Patient Vignette: "David"

David is a 34-year-old African man who has been in a relationship with his partner, Maria, for three years. He is a parole officer, a job he once took pride in, believing it allowed him to offer second chances to men who, like himself, had made mistakes. He presents for therapy at the urging of his supervisor, who noticed a sharp decline in David's patience and focus at work.

David's trauma began about eighteen months ago. The first incident was a slap during an argument about money. He was stunned, but Maria apologized profusely, crying, saying she had just lost control. He believed her. He loved her. He told himself it was a one-time thing. But it wasn't. Over the next year, the slaps became shoves, the shoves became punches. He recalls a night when she threw a glass ashtray at his head; he ducked, and it shattered against the wall. He never fought back. He was raised to never hit a woman, and the shame of being a victim-a strong man, a man who enforces the law-was a heavier weight than the bruises.

He left twice. The first time, he stayed at a motel for three nights, but Maria called him dozens of times, leaving voicemails that shifted from screaming fury to desperate, childlike pleading. "You're the only one who understands me," she would say. "I'm nothing without you." He went back. The second time, he drove to his mother's house two hours away, but he couldn't explain why he was there. The shame was a physical thing, a hot stone in his throat. He told his mother he had a stomach bug. He went back to Maria after a week.

Now, David lives in a state of constant, low-grade vigilance. He describes it as "waiting for the other shoe to drop." He cannot relax at home. He finds himself scanning the room for objects she could throw, noting the weight of a book, the sharp edge of a picture frame. He sleeps in fits, often jolting awake at the sound of a car door outside or the creak of the floorboards, his heart hammering. He has started sleeping on the couch, a decision he justified to Maria as "back pain." The truth is, he cannot bear to be that close to her in the dark, vulnerable.

His work has suffered. As a parole officer, he was known for his calm, measured demeanor. Now, he is irritable and hypervigilant with his clients. He misinterprets a slow response as defiance, a nervous laugh as mockery. Last month, he grabbed a client by the collar for failing a drug test, a violation of protocol that earned him a formal warning. He felt a surge of adrenaline, a flash of the same rage he feels toward Maria, but he cannot express it at home. He replays the argument that preceded the ashtray incident in his head constantly, wondering what he said wrong, how he could have de-escalated it, how he could have been better.

He avoids his friends, who used to come over to watch football. He avoids his family, who might ask about his relationship. He has stopped going to the gym, a place he once loved, because the sight of his own body in the mirror reminds him of the fading bruises. He feels hollow, disconnected from the confident man he used to be. He told me, "I'm a parole officer. I'm supposed to be the one who keeps people safe. But I can't even keep myself safe in my own home." The core of his world, the place that should be a sanctuary, is the source of his deepest fear. He feels trapped, not by a locked door, but by a love he cannot reconcile with the terror it now brings him.
